## The decision this serves

You inherited a dataset and a one-line methods section. Decide which of the patterns you are
looking at are analysis artifacts, before you attribute any of them to biology.

::: {.callout-important}
**Scale.** Runs in about 3 min, peak memory under 1 GB. Watch **comparisons of counts
across sections cut at different thicknesses** — that is the comparison that stops being
valid without warning.
:::

## Concept

A count matrix looks like a measurement. It is the output of a chain of physical decisions,
most made by someone else, several unrecorded, all still present in the numbers.

This is not a protocol. You will not learn incubation times here and you should not want to
— those live in vendor documentation and change between chemistry versions. What you need is
a model of which bench decision produces which analysis artifact.

### Fixation, which is a fork in the road

Formalin fixes tissue by crosslinking, and the same chemistry fragments RNA. That is
inherent, not a handling failure — which is why RNA integrity number cannot be applied to
FFPE material at all, since every RNA species in it is already fragmented. The metric used
instead is **DV200**, the percentage of fragments longer than 200 nucleotides.

The magnitudes are large. In a direct comparison of cardiac tissue, FFPE RNA had median RIN
2.5 and DV200 48%, against RIN 8.1 and DV200 97% for fresh and frozen
[@ffpe_ff_cardiac_2023]. Fragmentation is why FFPE workflows are probe-based: targeted
probes tolerate short fragments, while capture of intact polyadenylated transcripts does
not.

Platform requirements follow from this and are specific. Visium requires RIN above 7.0 for
fresh frozen and DV200 above 50% for FFPE; Xenium is FFPE with a DV200 threshold, and
optimal section thickness is **5 µm for FFPE and 10 µm for fresh frozen**
[@vai_spatial_specs].

Block age matters more than most people expect. In one benchmarking study, FFPE skin blocks
from 2018 averaged DV200 around 70% while blocks from 2008 averaged 31% — and lower initial
RNA quality yielded decreased unique gene counts [@ffpe_st_benchmark_2023]. If your archive
spans a decade and your conditions were collected in different years, RNA quality is
confounded with condition.

The operational consequence is blunt, and the cardiac comparison states it directly: refrain
from comparing gene expression between tissues with different storage conditions
[@ffpe_ff_cardiac_2023]. FFPE also distorts specific transcript classes rather than
uniformly attenuating everything — a subset of mitochondrial transcripts appeared falsely
overexpressed in FFPE relative to fresh and frozen [@ffpe_ff_cardiac_2023]. So the artifact
is not a scaling factor you can normalise away.

### Sectioning

Thickness sets how much of each cell lies in the plane, which sets counts per cell. A 10 µm
section and a 5 µm section from the same block yield systematically different totals — and
the recommended thickness differs by fixation type [@vai_spatial_specs], so a study mixing
FFPE and fresh-frozen material is also mixing thicknesses.

If those two sections are your two conditions, you have measured the cryostat.

### Permeabilisation and capture

Efficiency is not uniform across a section. Dense tissue, fibrotic regions and areas near a
fold behave differently, so capture efficiency varies spatially — and spatially varying
efficiency is indistinguishable, in the matrix alone, from a spatially varying expression
gradient.

This is the artifact with the worst possible shape. It is spatially autocorrelated, which
means it is exactly what the tests in lesson 12 are built to detect, and they will detect
it.

### Imaging, decoding, registration, segmentation

Depth and cycle count differ between runs; these are the ordinary batch effects. Decoding
assigns transcripts to positions and registration ties them to morphology — misregistration
moves cells into the wrong anatomical compartment while leaving their expression untouched,
which lesson 6 is entirely about. Segmentation, lesson 7, is the last decision before the
object you were handed.

### What the methods section will tell you

In practice, two or three of these. Platform and chemistry version are almost always
recorded. Section thickness sometimes. Time to fixation, permeabilisation conditions,
segmentation parameters and software versions usually are not.

So the first analysis on an inherited dataset is not clustering. It is reading the run
metadata and writing down which decisions you know and which you are assuming. The ones you
are assuming are your list of alternative explanations, and you will want it in writing
before you become attached to a result.

**The assumption that breaks first.** That the matrix you were handed is a measurement
rather than the output of a dozen decisions nobody wrote down.

## Runnable notebook

Read the run metadata of a toy dataset and reconstruct what was done.

Data tier: **Committed toy**

::: {.callout-warning}
**Not yet executed.** No output shown and nothing cached.
:::

```{python}
#| label: reconstruct
import spatialdata as sd

sdata = sd.read_zarr("data/cache/toy_section.zarr")

DECISIONS = [
    "fixation", "section_thickness_um", "permeabilisation",
    "chemistry_version", "registration_method", "segmentation_method",
    "dv200", "rin", "block_year",
]
known   = {k: sdata.attrs.get(k) for k in DECISIONS}
unknown = [k for k, v in known.items() if v is None]

for k, v in known.items():
    print(f"{k:<24} {v if v is not None else '— NOT RECORDED —'}")
print("\nalternative explanations you cannot rule out:", unknown)
```

```{python}
#| label: assert-metadata
# Delete a metadata field on purpose and confirm this fails rather than
# silently defaulting. Silent defaults are how these decisions disappear.

assert known["section_thickness_um"] is not None, (
    "thickness unrecorded: counts per cell are not comparable across sections"
)

# Thickness must match before any count-based comparison across sections.
thicknesses = {s: m["section_thickness_um"] for s, m in per_section.items()}
assert len(set(thicknesses.values())) == 1, (
    f"sections cut at different thicknesses: {thicknesses}"
)

# Fixation must match too — FFPE and fresh frozen are effectively different assays,
# and the published advice is not to compare across storage conditions at all.
assert len({m["fixation"] for m in per_section.values()}) == 1, (
    "mixed fixation: these sections should not be compared directly"
)
```

## Rosetta panel

Run metadata lives in the vendor output rather than in either ecosystem's object model, so
both languages read the same files.

```r
library(jsonlite)

meta <- fromJSON("data/cache/toy_section/experiment.xenium")
str(meta, max.level = 1)

decisions <- c("fixation", "section_thickness_um", "permeabilisation",
               "chemistry_version", "registration_method", "segmentation_method")
setdiff(decisions, names(meta))   # what is not recorded
```

## Failure mode

**What it produces.** Two sections cut at different thicknesses. Cells in the thicker section
capture more transcripts, cluster separately, and read as a distinct high-expression state.

A second version is worse because it is harder to see: two conditions collected years apart
from an FFPE archive, where block age has driven DV200 from around 70% to around 31%
[@ffpe_st_benchmark_2023]. Lower RNA quality reduces unique gene counts, so the older
condition looks transcriptionally quieter. That is a storage artifact wearing the costume of
a biological finding.

**The diagnostic that catches it.** Plot total counts per cell by section against recorded
thickness, fixation type and block year before interpreting any count difference. If a
technical variable explains it, you have found a knife setting or an archive, not a cell
state.

## Self-check

### Question 1

Which of the pipeline steps does your methods section actually record?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Usually platform and chemistry version, sometimes thickness, rarely anything else. Time to
fixation, permeabilisation conditions and segmentation parameters are the three most
consequential omissions.

Write down what you know. The remainder is your list of alternative explanations, and you
want it in writing before you are attached to a result.
:::

### Question 2

Your two conditions came from FFPE blocks archived eight years apart. What have you
measured?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Condition and RNA quality together, inseparably. Block age drives DV200 substantially —
around 70% for recent blocks against 31% for decade-old ones in one study — and lower
initial quality reduces unique gene counts [@ffpe_st_benchmark_2023].

The published advice is not to compare across storage conditions at all
[@ffpe_ff_cardiac_2023]. If you must, measure DV200 per block, put it in the model, and
state plainly that condition and quality are confounded. That is a limitation, not a
correction.
:::

### Question 3

A cluster appears in one section and not the other. What do you check first?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Total counts per cell in each section, against recorded thickness and cells recovered. If
the cluster is defined by overall expression level rather than by specific markers, you are
probably looking at a capture or thickness difference.

That check costs one plot and rules out the most common artifact. Check it before anything
biological.
:::

## Going further

What the platform can measure at all is lesson 5. Segmentation, the last step before your
matrix, is lesson 7. The statistical consequence of spatially varying capture efficiency is
lesson 12.

Deliberately omitted: bench execution. Buffers, incubation times and instrument settings
belong to the vendor protocol and change between chemistry versions faster than a tutorial
can honestly track.
